facts.fact: A rainbow is actually a full circle; the ground simply cuts off the bottom. From a plane you can see the entire ring.
facts.angle: reframes something everyone thinks they know
facts.whatif: What if you could get high enough off the ground? From a plane or a mountaintop you'd see the rainbow as a complete 360-degree circle, glowing at a fixed 42 degrees around the point opposite the Sun.
facts.wow: A rainbow isn't an object with a location, it's an angle, so every person is looking at their own private rainbow made by different raindrops.

facts.fact: Your stomach lining rebuilds itself every few days, because the hydrochloric acid inside is strong enough that the stomach would otherwise digest itself.
facts.angle: your own body is doing something alarming right now
facts.whatif: What if your stomach stopped making fresh lining? The hydrochloric acid at a pH of about 1.5 would start digesting your own stomach wall, which is exactly what a bleeding ulcer is.
facts.wow: That acid is strong enough to dissolve a razor blade or a nail, yet a fresh layer of protective cells rebuilds the wall every 3 to 4 days.

facts.fact: You are up to a couple of centimetres taller in the morning than at night, because the soft discs in your spine compress under your weight all day.
facts.angle: a hidden daily change in your own body
facts.whatif: What if gravity never pressed on you? It happens to astronauts, whose spinal discs decompress in zero gravity, so they grow up to 5 centimetres taller in space before shrinking back on Earth.
facts.wow: Over a single day your spinal discs slowly squeeze out water and lose up to 2 centimetres of height, then soak it back overnight while you sleep.

facts.fact: A single teaspoon of a neutron star would weigh roughly a billion tons, because its matter is crushed almost beyond belief.
facts.angle: a number that sounds fake but is true
facts.whatif: What if a teaspoon of a neutron star appeared in your hand? At a billion tons it would punch straight through the floor, through the Earth, and keep falling toward the planet's core.
facts.wow: The star packs more mass than our Sun into a ball the size of a city, and some spin over 700 times every single second.

facts.fact: A day on Venus is longer than its year: one rotation takes 243 Earth days, while one trip around the Sun takes only 225.
facts.whatif: What if you tried to live out a single year on Venus? You wouldn't even finish one day, because a Venus day of 243 Earth days outlasts its 225-day year.
facts.wow: Venus also spins in retrograde, the opposite direction to almost every other planet, so the Sun there rises in the west and sets in the east.

facts.fact: Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in water; its average density is only 0.687 grams per cubic centimetre, less than water itself.
facts.whatif: What if you found a bathtub big enough? Saturn would bob on the surface like a beach ball, because at 0.687 grams per cubic centimetre it is less dense than water.
facts.wow: Saturn is a ball of mostly hydrogen and helium with no solid surface, so there is nothing to stand on beneath its clouds.

facts.fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther away, which is the only reason they look the same size and we get perfect eclipses.
facts.angle: a cosmic coincidence you never noticed
facts.whatif: What if the Moon were slightly closer or farther? The perfect match, 400 times smaller but 400 times nearer, would break, and total eclipses would simply never happen.
facts.wow: The Moon drifts about 3.8 centimetres farther away every year, so in a few hundred million years total eclipses will vanish from the sky forever.

facts.fact: On Neptune and Uranus it likely rains solid diamonds, as extreme pressure squeezes carbon in the atmosphere into crystals.
facts.whatif: What if you could stand under the sky of Neptune? Crushing pressure would squeeze carbon into solid diamonds that fall like hail, so it literally rains gemstones.
facts.wow: Those diamonds may sink for thousands of kilometres and pool into a slushy ocean of liquid diamond deep inside the planet.

facts.fact: We have mapped more of the surface of Mars than the floor of our own oceans; most of the deep sea has never been seen.
facts.angle: the unknown is right here, not in space
facts.whatif: What if you could drain every ocean overnight? You'd reveal Earth's tallest mountain range and canyons deeper than any on land, terrain that over 80 percent of which no human has ever seen.
facts.wow: More people have walked on the Moon than have reached the deepest point of the ocean floor.

facts.fact: Everest is the highest point above sea level, but Mauna Kea in Hawaii is the tallest mountain on Earth measured from its base on the ocean floor.
facts.angle: the famous answer is technically wrong
facts.whatif: What if you measured mountains from their true base instead of sea level? Everest loses its crown to Mauna Kea, which stands over 10,000 metres tall, most of it hidden underwater.
facts.wow: From base to summit Mauna Kea is more than 1,000 metres taller than Everest, but you only ever see the top 4,000 metres above the waves.

facts.fact: Atoms are almost entirely empty space; if you removed it all, the entire human race would fit inside a single sugar cube.
facts.whatif: What if you squeezed the empty space out of every human on Earth? All 8 billion of us would pack down into a single sugar cube.
facts.wow: The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller than the atom around it, so if an atom were a stadium, the nucleus would be a single pea at the centre.

facts.fact: Time runs very slightly faster for your head than your feet, because gravity is weaker further from Earth, and it has been measured with atomic clocks.
facts.angle: time bends inside your own body
facts.whatif: What if you spent your whole life lying flat instead of standing? Your head and feet would age at almost the same rate, because standing up, your head genuinely ages faster than your feet.
facts.wow: Scientists proved it with atomic clocks raised just 33 centimetres apart, though over an 80-year lifetime your head gains only about 90 billionths of a second.

facts.fact: The tardigrade, a microscopic animal, can survive being frozen, boiled, crushed, and even the vacuum of outer space.
facts.whatif: What if you left a tardigrade in the open vacuum of space? It would survive by entering cryptobiosis, shrugging off radiation 1,000 times what would kill you and temperatures near absolute zero.
facts.wow: It pulls in its legs and dries into a glass-like husk called a tun, dropping its metabolism to almost zero and waiting, sometimes for decades, for water to return.

facts.fact: The mantis shrimp punches so fast it boils the water around its claw, creating a flash of light and heat.
facts.whatif: What if the mantis shrimp's punch actually misses its target? It barely matters, because the collapsing cavitation bubble left behind strikes a second time, flashing to nearly 20,000 degrees.
facts.wow: The punch accelerates faster than a bullet, over 10,000 g, and the collapsing bubble briefly glows with real light hotter than the surface of the Sun.

facts.fact: Honey never spoils; sealed honey found in 3,000-year-old Egyptian tombs was still perfectly edible.
facts.whatif: What if you ate honey sealed inside an Egyptian tomb 3,000 years ago? It would be perfectly safe to eat, because honey is one food that essentially never spoils.
facts.wow: Honey is so low in water and so acidic that bacteria die in it, and bees add an enzyme that produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide as a preservative.

facts.fact: If you laid out all the blood vessels in your body end to end, they would wrap around the entire Earth roughly two and a half times.
facts.whatif: What if you could unspool every blood vessel in your body into a single line? The roughly 60,000 miles of them would circle the entire Earth more than twice.
facts.wow: Most of that staggering length is capillaries so narrow that your blood cells have to squeeze through them single file.

facts.fact: Your nerves carry signals to your brain at speeds of up to about 270 miles per hour, faster than a Formula 1 car.
facts.angle: your body is faster than you think
facts.whatif: What if your nerves fired even a little slower? You already feel a stubbed toe a beat late, because touch races to your brain at up to 270 miles per hour while pain crawls on slower nerve fibres.
facts.wow: That's about 120 metres every second, quicker than a Formula 1 car at full throttle, all happening inside your own body.

facts.fact: The footprints left on the Moon will likely last millions of years, because there is no wind or water to erase them.
facts.whatif: What if you returned to the Moon a million years from now? Neil Armstrong's footprints would almost certainly still be there, because there is no wind or water to wear them away.
facts.wow: With no atmosphere to erode anything, the flags, the rover tracks, and every bootprint may outlast most human monuments on Earth.

facts.fact: Space is completely silent; sound needs a material to travel through, and space is a near-perfect vacuum, so no sound can exist.
facts.whatif: What if you screamed at the top of your lungs in space? No one could ever hear it, because sound needs a medium to travel and space is a near-perfect vacuum.
facts.wow: A star can explode as a supernova with the energy of billions of Suns and make absolutely no sound at all.

facts.fact: The sunlight hitting your skin left the Sun about eight minutes ago, so you are always seeing the Sun as it was in the past.
facts.angle: you live slightly in the past
facts.whatif: What if the Sun simply switched off right this second? You wouldn't know for about eight minutes, because that's how long its light takes to travel to your eyes.
facts.wow: Every time you look at the Sun you are seeing it as it was eight minutes and twenty seconds in the past, never as it is right now.

facts.fact: There are more stars in the observable universe than there are grains of sand on every beach on Earth combined.
facts.whatif: What if you counted every single grain of sand on every beach on Earth? You'd still fall short, because the universe holds far more stars than that, by thousands of times over.
facts.wow: The best estimates put the count near a 1 followed by 24 zeros, a number so large your brain physically cannot picture it.

facts.fact: Glass is not a slow-moving liquid; old windows are thicker at the bottom because of how they were made, not because glass flows.
facts.whatif: What if you waited a thousand years for a window to droop and pool at the bottom? It never would, because glass is an amorphous solid, not a slow-moving liquid.
facts.wow: Those uneven old windows look thicker at the base only because they were made by hand and installed heavy-side-down, not because the glass slid.

facts.fact: A blue whale's heart weighs about 400 pounds, and each beat pushes roughly 60 gallons of blood.
facts.angle: scale of the largest animal ever
facts.whatif: What if you could stand next to a blue whale's beating heart? It's the size of a small car, around 400 pounds, and each beat moves about 60 gallons of blood.
facts.wow: That heartbeat is so powerful it can be detected from about two miles away underwater.

facts.fact: Some turtles can breathe through their rear ends, absorbing oxygen through their tissues to survive long winters underwater.
facts.whatif: What if a pond froze solid all winter and a turtle was trapped beneath the ice? It would simply breathe through its rear end, pulling oxygen from the water through an opening called the cloaca.
facts.wow: This is called cloacal respiration, and for some turtles it supplies most of the oxygen they need to survive months underwater without surfacing.

facts.fact: A hummingbird's heart can beat over 1,200 times per minute, and they are the only birds that can fly backwards.
facts.angle: extreme engineering in a tiny body
facts.whatif: What if your heart beat like a hummingbird's? At over 1,200 beats a minute you'd have to eat almost constantly just to survive, which is exactly what a hummingbird does.
facts.wow: Its wings beat up to 80 times a second, letting it hover in place and become the only bird on Earth that can truly fly backwards.

facts.fact: You shed tens of thousands of dead skin cells every minute, and much of the dust in your home is actually made of you.
facts.whatif: What if you tracked where all your dead skin actually ends up? A large share of the house dust drifting through your home is you, because you shed tens of thousands of dead skin cells every minute.
facts.wow: You replace your entire outer layer of skin roughly every two to four weeks, losing around a full pound of skin cells each year.

facts.fact: About 8 million lightning bolts strike the Earth every single day, roughly 100 every second.
facts.whatif: What if you could see every lightning strike on Earth at once? The planet is hit by about 8 million bolts a day, which works out to roughly 100 every single second.
facts.wow: That means somewhere on Earth, right now as you watch this, lightning is striking about a hundred times over.

facts.fact: There is a vast cloud in space, Sagittarius B2, containing enough alcohol to dwarf anything on Earth, drifting near the center of our galaxy.
facts.whatif: What if you could bottle a cloud in space? Sagittarius B2, near the center of our galaxy, holds enough alcohol to dwarf every drop that has ever existed on Earth.
facts.wow: It's mostly undrinkable methanol and vinyl alcohol, not the kind in a drink, but the sheer quantity is billions of billions of times anything on our planet.

facts.fact: Bananas are slightly radioactive because they contain potassium-40, a naturally radioactive isotope; a single banana gives a dose of about 0.1 microsieverts.
facts.whatif: What would actually happen if you ate a million bananas at once? You'd die from the potassium itself, ordinary potassium poisoning that stops your heart, long before the radiation from potassium-40 ever mattered.
facts.wow: You are more radioactive than the banana; your own body fires roughly 5,000 potassium-40 decays every single second, and your kidneys flush the extra potassium so the dose never adds up.

facts.fact: Your heart beats around 100,000 times a day, pumping blood through your body without ever taking a single break.
facts.whatif: What if your heart took a single day off in your entire life? It never does; it beats about 100,000 times a day, every day, from before you're born until the moment you die.
facts.wow: Over an average lifetime that's roughly 2.5 billion beats, pushing around 2,000 gallons of blood through you every single day.

facts.fact: If you were exposed to space without a suit, you would not freeze solid or explode; you'd stay conscious for about 15 seconds before the oxygen leaves your blood.
facts.angle: the movies got it completely wrong
facts.whatif: What if an airlock burst open and flung you into space? You wouldn't pop like a balloon; you'd have about 15 conscious seconds before a lack of oxygen knocks you out.
facts.wow: The vacuum causes ebullism, where the water in your body starts to boil at your own temperature, and a NASA test subject in 1966 felt the saliva bubbling on his tongue before he blacked out.

facts.fact: The immortal jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, can reverse its own life cycle, reverting to a juvenile form when injured or old and starting over, potentially forever.
facts.whatif: What if aging had a reset button? This jellyfish has one; facing death, Turritopsis dohrnii transforms its own cells back into a baby polyp and begins its entire life again.
facts.wow: It does this through transdifferentiation, essentially a butterfly turning back into a caterpillar, which makes it the only animal known to be biologically immortal.

facts.fact: There is a region of space called the Bootes void, about 330 million light-years across and almost completely empty, a giant hole in the universe.
facts.angle: the emptiest place we know of
facts.whatif: What if our galaxy floated in the middle of the Bootes void? The night sky would look almost starless, because the nearest galaxies would be hundreds of millions of light-years away.
facts.wow: This bubble of nothing is 330 million light-years across yet holds only a few dozen galaxies, where thousands should be; if we lived inside it, we might not have discovered other galaxies existed until the 1960s.

facts.fact: The Andromeda galaxy is the farthest thing you can see with the naked eye, and its light left 2.5 million years ago, so you are literally seeing into the deep past.
facts.angle: you can see time travel with your own eyes
facts.whatif: What if Andromeda vanished completely tonight? You would keep seeing it in the sky for 2.5 million more years, because that's how long its light takes to reach your naked eye.
facts.wow: The light landing on your eye tonight left Andromeda before modern humans existed, back when our ancestors were first chipping stone tools.

facts.fact: At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, the water presses down at about 8 tons per square inch, over 1,000 times the pressure at the surface.
facts.angle: a crushing world right below us
facts.whatif: What if you dived to the bottom of the Mariana Trench without protection? The pressure of about 8 tons per square inch would crush your lungs and collapse your body almost instantly.
facts.wow: That's like balancing dozens of jumbo jets on your body, yet delicate creatures like the snailfish live down there perfectly happily.

facts.fact: Most of your body is only a few years old because you constantly replace billions of cells, but the neurons in your brain and the lenses of your eyes are as old as you are.
facts.angle: you are and aren't the same person you were
facts.whatif: What if you're basically a brand-new person every few years? Almost, but not entirely; the neurons in your brain and the lenses of your eyes are never replaced, staying exactly as old as you are.
facts.wow: Your skeleton fully renews itself about every 10 years and your gut lining every few days, yet you carry the same original brain cells your whole life.

facts.fact: The DNA in a single one of your cells would stretch about 2 metres if uncoiled, and all the DNA in your body laid end to end would reach the Sun and back many times.
facts.whatif: What if you unravelled the DNA from every cell in your body and laid it in one line? It would stretch to the Sun and back dozens of times over.
facts.wow: Each microscopic cell packs about 2 metres of DNA folded into a space you could never see with the naked eye, multiplied across tens of trillions of cells.

facts.fact: The giant squid has the largest eye of any animal, up to about 25 centimetres across, roughly the size of a dinner plate, evolved to catch the faint glow stirred up by a hunting sperm whale.
facts.angle: an eye built like an early-warning system
facts.whatif: What if you needed to spot a predator in pitch darkness a football field away? A giant squid can; its eye, about 25 centimetres across, is built to catch the faint bioluminescent stir of a sperm whale swimming up to 120 metres off, buying it just enough warning to flee.
facts.wow: That's roughly triple the width of a human eye, and the next largest eye in the ocean, a swordfish's, is barely a third of the size.

facts.fact: The giant tube worm Riftia pachyptila has no mouth or gut at all; it survives entirely on bacteria living inside it that turn the toxic hydrogen sulfide pouring from deep-sea hydrothermal vents into food.
facts.angle: an animal that never eats a single meal
facts.whatif: What if an animal never had to eat a bite its whole life? The giant tube worm Riftia pachyptila doesn't; with no mouth or gut, it lives entirely off bacteria inside it that turn a hydrothermal vent's toxic hydrogen sulfide into food.
facts.wow: Those bacteria can make up as much as 50 percent of its body weight, and its blood-red plume is red because it's packed with hemoglobin, ferrying oxygen and sulfide down to feed them.

facts.fact: Mercury has the wildest temperature swings of any planet: daytime surface heat reaches about 430 degrees Celsius, while at night it plunges to about minus 180 Celsius.
facts.angle: the planet closest to the Sun is also brutally cold
facts.whatif: What if you stood on Mercury as the Sun set? Within hours the ground would cool from a scorching 430 degrees Celsius to a frozen minus 180 Celsius, the biggest day-to-night temperature swing of any planet in the solar system.
facts.wow: Mercury sits closest to the Sun, yet Venus is actually the hotter planet overall, because Mercury has almost no atmosphere left to trap any of that heat once night falls.

facts.fact: Muons created when cosmic rays strike the upper atmosphere have a lifespan of just 2.2 microseconds, far too short to fall 15 kilometres to the ground, yet at near light speed, time dilation lets billions of them reach the surface anyway.
facts.angle: relativity proving itself over your head right now
facts.whatif: What if a clock ticking near light speed actually ran slower? A muon's does; born 15 kilometres up with only 2.2 microseconds to live, it should decay long before reaching the ground, but relativistic time dilation stretches that lifespan just enough for it to survive the fall.
facts.wow: About one of these muons passes through every square centimetre of ground every minute, meaning a real proof of Einstein's relativity is quietly raining down on you right now.

facts.fact: The liver can regenerate itself: after a living donor gives away as much as 65 percent of it for a transplant, both the donor's remaining liver and the piece given to the recipient regrow to nearly full size within about 8 to 10 weeks.
facts.angle: the one organ that grows itself back
facts.whatif: What if you cut away most of an organ and expected it to just grow back? A liver donor's does; after giving up as much as 65 percent of it, the remaining tissue regenerates to nearly full size and function within about 8 to 10 weeks.
facts.wow: It's the only solid organ in the body that can do this, regrowing real working tissue instead of just scarring over, which is exactly why living-donor liver transplants are possible.

facts.fact: The human body emits a faint visible glow of light, invisible to the naked eye but caught by an ultra-sensitive camera in a 2009 study, and its brightness rises and falls on a daily rhythm, peaking in the afternoon.
facts.angle: you glow like a firefly, just too dimly to see
facts.whatif: What if your body glowed like a firefly, just too dimly to notice? It does; a 2009 study used a camera cooled to nearly minus 120 degrees Celsius to catch the light and found it's about 1,000 times too faint for the naked eye to ever see.
facts.wow: The glow isn't constant either; these biophotons brighten and dim across the day in step with your circadian rhythm, peaking in the afternoon around your cheeks and forehead.

facts.fact: The axolotl can regrow an entire missing limb, complete with bone, muscle, and nerves, in about 40 to 50 days, and it can also regenerate damaged spinal cord and parts of its heart and brain without forming any scar tissue.
facts.angle: an animal that heals like a reset button
facts.whatif: What if losing a leg were just a temporary inconvenience? For the axolotl it is; sever one of its limbs and a fully functional replacement, bone, muscle, and nerves included, regrows in about 40 to 50 days, with no scar left behind.
facts.wow: It can also regenerate damaged spinal cord and even parts of its own heart and brain, which is why labs around the world keep colonies of them alive just to study how it's done.

facts.fact: Naked mole rats can survive about 18 minutes with no oxygen at all by switching their metabolism to burn fructose instead of glucose, and they are also remarkably resistant to cancer, living over 30 years despite being mouse-sized.
facts.angle: a rodent that breaks the rules of biology
facts.whatif: What if an animal's brain could just switch fuels when the oxygen ran out? A naked mole rat's does; starved of air, it burns fructose instead of glucose, letting it survive about 18 minutes with no oxygen at all.
facts.wow: That trick works in its heart and brain too, not just the gut like in other mammals, and on top of it naked mole rats almost never develop cancer, living over 30 years, ten times longer than a mouse their size.

facts.fact: A woodpecker's head decelerates at roughly 1,000 times the force of gravity with every peck, tens of times harder than a hit that would concuss a person, yet its tiny, lightweight brain is simply too small for that force to cause damage.
facts.angle: an animal that headbangs a tree without injury
facts.whatif: What if you slammed your head into a tree trunk 20 times a second? You'd be concussed instantly, but a woodpecker isn't; each strike decelerates its head at roughly 1,000 times the force of gravity, yet its tiny, lightweight brain is simply too small for that force to cause damage.
facts.wow: A 2022 study found the skull acts like a stiff hammer, not a cushion, and even the hardest hits stay well below the threshold that would concuss a primate brain.

facts.fact: Aerogel, nicknamed frozen smoke, is up to 99.8 percent air by volume, making it the lightest solid material ever created, yet a thin sheet of it can protect a bare hand from the flame of a blowtorch held right against it.
facts.angle: a solid that is almost entirely empty air
facts.whatif: What if you could hold a blowtorch flame directly against your palm? With a thin layer of aerogel in between you actually could, because this solid, nicknamed frozen smoke, is up to 99.8 percent air yet still blocks heat well enough to protect skin at point-blank range.
facts.wow: Despite being almost entirely empty space, aerogel holds more than a dozen Guinness World Records for its extremes, including the lightest solid ever produced.

facts.fact: Earth's solid inner core runs about 5,400 degrees Celsius, roughly as hot as the surface of the Sun, and it stays solid only because the crushing pressure at the centre of the planet keeps iron from melting.
facts.angle: the middle of our planet is as hot as a star
facts.whatif: What if the centre of the Earth were somehow cooler than we think? It isn't; the inner core runs about 5,400 degrees Celsius, roughly matching the Sun's surface, and it only stays solid because the pressure down there is extreme enough to stop iron from melting despite the heat.
facts.wow: That means the ball of solid iron at the middle of our planet is, temperature for temperature, about as hot as the glowing surface of the star we orbit.

facts.fact: Much of the gold on Earth was forged in the collision of neutron stars, the most violent explosions in the universe, long before the Sun existed.
facts.angle: an everyday object with an unimaginably violent origin
facts.whatif: What if you could trace your wedding ring back to its birth? Every gold atom in it was hammered into existence when two dead stars slammed together and briefly outshone entire galaxies.
facts.wow: The gold in your jewelry is older than the Sun and was made in an explosion so powerful it bent the fabric of space itself.

facts.fact: Water is one of the only substances that expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats and why freezing water can shatter solid rock.
facts.angle: a familiar substance that breaks a basic rule
facts.whatif: What if ice sank instead of floated? Lakes and oceans would freeze solid from the bottom up, and almost nothing could survive a winter.
facts.wow: The same quirk that makes ice float is the reason a bottle of water can burst in your freezer and why potholes appear every spring.

facts.fact: That fresh smell after rain has a name, petrichor, and it comes partly from a compound called geosmin made by soil bacteria that your nose can detect at a few parts per trillion.
facts.angle: a familiar sensation with a hidden biological source
facts.whatif: What if you could out-smell a shark? For this one compound you already can, detecting geosmin at concentrations far too faint for most animals.
facts.wow: The smell of rain is really the scent of bacteria, and your nose is more sensitive to it than to almost anything else on Earth.

facts.fact: Raindrops are not teardrop-shaped. Small ones are near-perfect spheres, and large ones flatten into the shape of a hamburger bun before breaking apart.
facts.angle: corrects an image everyone draws wrong
facts.whatif: What if you drew a raindrop the way it really falls? It would look less like a tear and more like a tiny parachute being pushed flat by the air.
facts.wow: The classic teardrop raindrop doesn't exist in nature, it's flattened by the very air it falls through.

facts.fact: Earth's magnetic north and south poles have completely swapped places hundreds of times, and the last full flip was about 780,000 years ago.
facts.angle: the ground under you is less permanent than it feels
facts.whatif: What if your compass pointed south? For most of a past era it did, and one day it will again when the poles flip once more.
facts.wow: The record of these flips is frozen into the rock of the ocean floor like a barcode written by the planet itself.

facts.fact: The largest living thing on Earth is not a whale or a tree but a single fungus in Oregon that spreads across more than three square miles and may be thousands of years old.
facts.angle: the biggest organism is one you can barely see
facts.whatif: What if the biggest creature alive was hiding under a forest? It is, woven invisibly through the soil across an area larger than a thousand football fields.
facts.wow: Almost all of this giant lives underground as a web of threads, and most of it has never been seen by anyone.

facts.fact: Trees quietly trade sugar and send warning signals to each other through an underground network of fungi that scientists nicknamed the wood wide web.
facts.angle: a hidden social life beneath a silent forest
facts.whatif: What if a forest was really one connected community? A dying tree can pump its remaining sugar to its neighbors through the fungal threads linking their roots.
facts.wow: Beneath a quiet forest, trees are constantly sharing food and sounding alarms through a living underground internet.

facts.fact: Botanically, a banana is a berry, but a strawberry is not a berry at all.
facts.angle: the categories you learned are backwards
facts.whatif: What if the fruit aisle was lying to you? By the actual botanical rules, bananas, grapes and even watermelons are berries, while strawberries and raspberries are not.
facts.wow: The definition of a berry has nothing to do with size or seeds on the outside, which is why a banana qualifies and a strawberry doesn't.

facts.fact: Some species of bamboo grow almost a meter in a single day, fast enough that you could nearly watch it rise.
facts.angle: a plant moving at a visible speed
facts.whatif: What if a plant could outpace you? Certain bamboo shoots add height faster than a snail moves, climbing nearly a meter between sunrise and sunset.
facts.wow: Bamboo isn't a tree at all, it's a grass, and it's the fastest growing plant on the planet.

facts.fact: Sound travels more than four times faster through water than through air, which is how whales can call to each other across entire oceans.
facts.angle: a familiar sense behaving strangely in a new medium
facts.whatif: What if you shouted underwater? The sound would race away from you far faster than in air, but your ears would struggle to tell where it came from.
facts.wow: A whale's call can cross an ocean because sound moves through water at nearly a mile every second.

facts.fact: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa is the loudest sound in recorded history, heard 3,000 miles away, and its pressure wave circled the entire planet multiple times.
facts.angle: an event so extreme it broke the scale
facts.whatif: What if a sound could travel around the world? Krakatoa's did, its shockwave lapping the planet several times and registering on instruments everywhere.
facts.wow: The blast was so powerful that sailors 40 miles away had their eardrums ruptured, and it was heard across a thirteenth of the Earth.

facts.fact: In a room of just 23 people, there is a better than even chance that two of them share the same birthday.
facts.angle: an answer that feels impossible but is provably true
facts.whatif: What if you bet on a shared birthday in a small group? With only 23 people the odds are already in your favor, and with 70 it is almost certain.
facts.wow: Your intuition says you'd need hundreds of people, but the math only needs a couple of dozen because it counts every possible pair.

facts.fact: There are more viruses in a single liter of seawater than there are people on Earth, and most are completely harmless to us.
facts.angle: an invisible scale hiding in plain water
facts.whatif: What if you scooped up a bottle of seawater? You'd be holding more virus particles than the entire human population, quietly running the ocean's food web.
facts.wow: These ocean viruses aren't a threat, they recycle nutrients on a scale that helps keep the whole planet alive.

facts.fact: GPS satellites have to correct for Einstein's relativity. Their clocks tick faster than clocks on the ground, and without the fix your maps would drift off by miles every single day.
facts.angle: abstract physics running invisibly in daily life
facts.whatif: What if we ignored Einstein? Your phone's navigation would be wrong by about ten kilometers after just one day, useless for finding anything.
facts.wow: Every time you follow a map, your phone is silently accounting for the fact that time itself runs at different speeds in orbit.

facts.fact: Some metals can remember their shape. Bend them out of form, warm them up, and they snap back to exactly how they started.
facts.angle: a material that behaves like it's alive
facts.whatif: What if you could crumple a paperclip and have it heal itself? A shape-memory metal wire does exactly that the instant you add a little heat.
facts.wow: These metals are used in everything from bendable glasses frames to tiny stents that unfold inside the body once they reach body temperature.

facts.fact: A lightning bolt heats the air around it to roughly 30,000 kelvin, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
facts.angle: a stunning true comparison people repeat to sound smart
facts.whatif: What if you could take a lightning bolt's temperature? For a few millionths of a second its channel hits near 30,000 kelvin, roughly five times the Sun's surface, which sits around 5,800.
facts.wow: That sudden heat makes the air burst outward faster than sound, and the shockwave is exactly what you hear as thunder.

facts.fact: Weight for weight, spider dragline silk is stronger than steel and tougher than Kevlar.
facts.angle: a true fact that reframes a common everyday thing
facts.whatif: What if a strand of spider silk were as thick as a pencil? By weight it beats steel for strength and Kevlar for toughness, so that rope could soak up enormous force without snapping.
facts.wow: A spider spins this super-material at room temperature from water and protein, something no human factory can yet copy.

facts.fact: Tyrannosaurus rex lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus.
facts.angle: reframes how people picture deep time
facts.whatif: What if a T. rex could have met a Stegosaurus? It never could. Stegosaurus vanished about 150 million years ago and T. rex lived around 66 million years ago, a bigger gap than the one between T. rex and you.
facts.wow: The dinosaurs we imagine fighting side by side were often separated by more time than separates us from the last dinosaurs.

facts.fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the first Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
facts.angle: a true fact that rewires your sense of history
facts.whatif: What if Cleopatra picked the closer event, the pyramids or the Moon landing? The Great Pyramid was already about 2,500 years old in her lifetime, while the Moon landing was under 2,000 years after her, so the rockets win.
facts.wow: The pyramids were ancient history even to the ancient Egyptians we picture as their builders.

facts.fact: The largest desert on Earth is Antarctica. A desert is defined by how little water falls, not by heat.
facts.angle: reframes a word everyone thinks they understand
facts.whatif: What if you ranked deserts by size instead of temperature? Antarctica tops the list at about 14 million square kilometres, because almost no precipitation reaches its interior. It is a frozen polar desert.
facts.wow: Parts of Antarctica's Dry Valleys may not have seen rain for around two million years, making them some of the driest places on the planet.

facts.fact: The Hawaiian Islands are slowly drifting toward Japan, at about the speed your fingernails grow.
facts.angle: a slow true motion nobody notices
facts.whatif: What if you waited on Hawaii long enough? The Pacific Plate carries the islands northwest about 7 centimetres a year, so over millions of years today's islands sink and fresh ones rise over the same hotspot.
facts.wow: Hawaii is really a conveyor belt of volcanoes: the plate slides over a fixed hot spot and leaves a long trail of islands behind it.

facts.fact: The Sun's core is actually too cool for fusion. It only shines because of a quantum loophole.
facts.angle: reframes why the Sun works at all
facts.whatif: What if the rules were strictly classical? At about 15 million degrees the Sun's protons lack the energy to smash together over the Coulomb barrier, but quantum tunnelling lets them slip through occasionally, and that is why the Sun burns.
facts.wow: Without a strange effect that lets particles cheat through walls, the stars, and we, would not exist.

facts.fact: Most of what you call taste is really smell. Pinch your nose and food loses much of its flavour.
facts.angle: reframes a sense you use every day
facts.whatif: What if you ate with your nose pinched shut? Your tongue reports only five basic tastes, so up to about 80 percent of a food's flavour, which really comes from smell drifting up the back of your throat, simply disappears.
facts.wow: It is why food tastes flat with a cold, and why most people cannot name a jelly bean's flavour with their nose held.

facts.fact: In 2016 scientists found a bacterium that had evolved to eat plastic bottles.
facts.whatif: What if a microbe learned to digest our rubbish? One found at a Japanese recycling site in 2016, Ideonella sakaiensis, makes an enzyme that breaks down PET, the plastic in drink bottles, and eats it for food.
facts.wow: Engineered versions of its enzyme can now break a plastic bottle apart in hours, hinting at a real future for recycling.

facts.fact: At least half of the oxygen you breathe comes from the ocean, not from forests.
facts.angle: reframes where our air really comes from
facts.whatif: What if forests were not the main source of our air? Tiny drifting phytoplankton in the sea make at least half of Earth's oxygen, and one kind, Prochlorococcus, may be the most abundant photosynthetic living thing on the planet.
facts.wow: Roughly every second breath you take comes from microscopic sea life most people have never heard of.

facts.fact: Sharks are older than trees. They have existed for about 450 million years.
facts.angle: reframes how ancient a familiar animal really is
facts.whatif: What if you lined up sharks and trees by age? Sharks win by a wide margin, swimming the oceans about 450 million years ago, roughly 90 million years before the first trees ever grew.
facts.wow: Sharks are also older than Saturn's rings and have survived all five mass extinctions that wiped out most life on Earth.

facts.fact: A shrimp can snap its claw so fast it boils the water and flashes light hotter than the sun's surface.
facts.angle: a tiny animal doing something physically absurd
facts.whatif: What if an animal could punch water hard enough to make it glow? The pistol shrimp does. Its claw snaps so fast it rips open a cavitation bubble that collapses at nearly 4,700 degrees, briefly close to the sun's surface, with a snap of light and sound.
facts.wow: The shockwave alone can stun or kill its prey, and the collective snapping of these shrimp is loud enough to interfere with submarine sonar.

facts.fact: Your body contains roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells, maybe more.
facts.angle: unsettling truth about what 'you' are made of
facts.whatif: What if you counted every cell you carry? Only about half would be yours. Your body holds around 38 trillion bacteria alongside roughly 30 trillion human cells.
facts.wow: Most of them live in your gut, and they help digest food, train your immune system, and even influence your mood.

facts.fact: Earth's days are slowly getting longer because the Moon is stealing its spin.
facts.angle: a slow cosmic theft happening right now
facts.whatif: What if a day wasn't always 24 hours? It wasn't. The Moon's pull drags on Earth and slows its spin by about 1.7 milliseconds per century, so dinosaurs lived days closer to 23 hours long.
facts.wow: Run it backward far enough and a day on the young Earth lasted only about six hours, with the Moon looming huge and close overhead.

facts.fact: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, and one heart stops whenever it swims.
facts.angle: an alien body plan hiding in the ocean
facts.whatif: What if your heart stopped every time you moved? For an octopus that's normal. It has three hearts, and the main one quits beating whenever it swims, which is why they often prefer to crawl.
facts.wow: Its blood is blue because it carries oxygen with copper-based hemocyanin instead of the iron that makes our blood red.

facts.fact: The Amazon rainforest is fertilized by dust blown across the Atlantic from the Sahara desert.
facts.whatif: What if the greenest place on Earth was fed by the emptiest? It is. Around 27 million tonnes of Saharan dust cross the Atlantic each year, and it carries the phosphorus the Amazon needs to grow.
facts.wow: Much of that dust comes from a single ancient dried lake bed in Chad, once full of life, now feeding a jungle an ocean away.

facts.fact: On one blue planet far away, it rains molten glass sideways in 8,000 kilometre per hour winds.
facts.angle: a hellish world that looks Earth-like from afar
facts.whatif: What if a deep blue planet wasn't blue from oceans? The planet HD 189733b is a rich blue, but its colour comes from clouds of silicate glass, and winds near 8,000 kilometres per hour whip that glass sideways as rain.
facts.wow: Those winds are about seven times the speed of sound, making its beautiful blue one of the deadliest sights in the galaxy.

facts.fact: Your brain runs on about 20 watts of power, less than a dim light bulb.
facts.angle: an everyday organ quietly outperforming machines
facts.whatif: What if you knew how little energy your thoughts cost? Your brain runs on roughly 20 watts, less than a dim light bulb, yet it out-thinks supercomputers that gulp down millions of times more power.
facts.wow: That single dim-bulb of power runs about 86 billion neurons firing in patterns we still can't fully copy.

facts.fact: The Eiffel Tower grows about 15 centimetres taller every summer.
facts.angle: a landmark quietly breathing with the seasons
facts.whatif: What if a landmark changed height with the weather? The Eiffel Tower does. Its iron expands in the summer heat, making the whole tower stand about 15 centimetres taller than it does in winter.
facts.wow: The same heat makes it lean slightly away from the sun, its top drifting a few centimetres as the day warms one side.

facts.fact: The mantis shrimp has 12 to 16 kinds of color receptor in its eyes, to our 3, yet it is actually worse than us at telling similar colors apart.
facts.angle: reverses a 'fact' the internet loves to repeat
facts.whatif: If the mantis shrimp has five times our color receptors, does it see a far richer world than we do? Astonishingly, no. Tests show it struggles to tell apart colors we find obvious, because its eyes scan like a barcode reader instead of blending colors the way ours do.
facts.wow: Each eye also sees in 3D on its own and can detect circular polarized light, a kind of light no other animal on Earth is known to see.

facts.fact: There are more possible games of chess than there are atoms in the observable universe.
facts.angle: how a simple game hides something bigger than reality
facts.whatif: A chessboard has only 64 squares, so how can it hold more games than the universe has atoms? Because the moves branch so fast that the count blows past a number with 120 zeros, while the universe has only about 80.
facts.wow: No computer will ever list them all. There is not enough matter in all of existence to even store the list.

facts.fact: When you eat fresh pineapple, it is digesting you back. It contains bromelain, an enzyme that breaks down protein, which is why your tongue can feel raw.
facts.angle: an everyday food that fights back
facts.whatif: Why does fresh pineapple make your mouth tingle or sting? Its enzyme is actually dissolving the surface protein of your tongue and cheeks. You just replace those cells fast enough not to notice.
facts.wow: Canned pineapple never does it, because heat destroys the enzyme. Only raw pineapple bites back.

facts.fact: Your eyes are so sensitive that, in the dark, they can register a single particle of light, one photon, the smallest amount of light that can exist.
facts.angle: the physical limit of human perception
facts.whatif: What is the faintest thing a human being can possibly see? Experiments show your eye can react to a single photon, so you are sensing light right at the edge of what physics even allows.
facts.wow: On a truly dark, clear night your eyes are sensitive enough that you could catch the light of a single candle flame from miles away.

facts.fact: In the vacuum of space, two pieces of the same bare metal pressed together will fuse into one solid piece, with no heat at all. It is called cold welding.
facts.angle: a hidden hazard of space engineering
facts.whatif: Why would metal parts weld together in space with no torch and no heat? On Earth a thin layer of air and oxide keeps metal surfaces apart. Remove the air, and clean metal cannot tell where one piece ends and the next begins.
facts.wow: This is a real engineering nightmare. Moving parts on spacecraft have jammed in orbit because they quietly welded themselves shut.

facts.fact: Identical twins share the exact same DNA, yet they have completely different fingerprints. Your prints are not written in your genes.
facts.angle: the part of you that no code decides
facts.whatif: If twins have identical DNA, why do their fingerprints never match? Because the ridges are shaped by tiny random forces as you press against the womb. Pure chance, not code, gives you the pattern on your fingertips.
facts.wow: It means the one mark police use to tell people apart is decided by randomness, not heredity, so not even your genes can predict it.

facts.fact: Gallium is a metal that melts in your hand. Its melting point is below body temperature, so a solid chunk turns to liquid just from your warmth.
facts.angle: a solid metal that behaves impossibly
facts.whatif: Could a piece of metal really melt just from being held? Gallium melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, cooler than your skin, so a solid spoon of it slowly collapses into a silver puddle in your palm.
facts.wow: You can cast a gallium spoon, stir it into hot tea, and watch the spoon vanish completely into the drink.

facts.fact: A single fluffy white cloud can weigh more than a million pounds, about the same as 100 elephants, yet it floats.
facts.angle: an everyday sight hiding an impossible weight
facts.whatif: If a cloud weighs as much as a hundred elephants, why does it not fall out of the sky? Its water is spread across billions of droplets so small that the warm air rising beneath easily holds them all up.
facts.wow: You are looking up at a swimming pool's worth of water hanging over your head, held there by nothing but rising air.

facts.fact: The longest running lab experiment in the world watches a blob of tar drip. It looks like a solid you could shatter with a hammer, but it is a liquid so thick it forms only about one drop per decade.
facts.angle: a solid that is secretly a liquid
facts.whatif: Is the tar in this jar a solid or a liquid? It shatters like glass if you hit it, yet it has been slowly flowing since 1927, dripping so rarely that for decades nobody managed to catch a single drop falling.
facts.wow: It is billions of times thicker than honey. A scientist who watched it for years died just months before a drop finally fell.

facts.fact: The world's spiders eat more meat every year than the entire human race does. Together they kill an estimated 400 to 800 million tons of prey annually.
facts.angle: an invisible appetite all around you
facts.whatif: Could the small creatures in the corners of your home really out-eat all of humanity? Yes. Add up every spider on Earth and the meat they catch each year outweighs all the meat and fish eaten by all people combined.
facts.wow: There are so many spiders that their combined weight is estimated at around 25 million tons, and you are almost never more than a few feet from one.

facts.fact: Helium was discovered on the Sun before it was ever found on Earth, which is why it is named after the Greek sun god, Helios.
facts.angle: an element found in the sky before the ground
facts.whatif: How do you discover something 93 million miles away before finding it at home? In 1868 astronomers split the Sun's light during an eclipse and saw a color that matched no known element. It was helium, and nobody isolated it on Earth for another 27 years.
facts.wow: The party balloon gas that makes your voice squeak was first spotted glowing in the atmosphere of a star.

facts.fact: The shortest war in recorded history lasted about 38 minutes. It was fought between Britain and Zanzibar in 1896 and was over before most people knew it had started.
facts.whatif: How long can a war between two countries possibly last? In 1896 one lasted under 40 minutes, ending in the time it takes to watch a sitcom, after a brief naval bombardment forced a surrender.
facts.wow: A single ceasefire in that war took longer to arrange than the fighting itself.

facts.fact: A Greenland shark swimming in the Arctic right now may have been born before the United States existed. They can live around 400 years, making them the longest-lived animals with a backbone.
facts.angle: a living animal that outlasts nations
facts.whatif: How old is the oldest fish in the ocean today? A Greenland shark alive now could have been swimming since the 1600s, meaning it was already a century old before America was even a country.
facts.wow: They grow only about a centimeter a year and do not even become adults until they are around 150 years old.

facts.fact: The Atlantic Ocean is getting wider every year, at about the same speed your fingernails grow. The Americas are drifting away from Europe and Africa.
facts.whatif: Is the distance between New York and London fixed? No. The seafloor between them splits open a little more each year, pushing the continents apart at roughly the rate your fingernails grow.
facts.wow: Iceland sits right on the crack, so you can literally stand with one foot on the North American plate and one on the European plate.

facts.fact: A giant tree is built mostly out of thin air. Most of its solid wood comes from carbon pulled out of the sky, not from the soil.
facts.angle: reframes something you walk past every day
facts.whatif: Where does the mass of a 100-ton tree actually come from? Not mostly the ground, as it feels like it should. Most of that wood is carbon the tree pulled straight out of the air as carbon dioxide.
facts.wow: So a forest is, in a real sense, sky turned solid, and burning it sends that captured air right back up.

facts.fact: In 1986 a calm lake in Cameroon suddenly exploded a cloud of invisible gas that silently suffocated more than 1,700 people in a single night.
facts.angle: a peaceful place hiding a lethal switch
facts.whatif: How could a still, quiet lake kill an entire region without a wave or a sound? For years it trapped volcanic carbon dioxide in its deep water, until one night the lake overturned and released it all at once, a heavy invisible blanket that smothered everything below it.
facts.wow: Engineers now keep giant pipes running in the lake around the clock, slowly venting the gas so it can never build up and burst again.

facts.fact: Go back only a few thousand years and every single person alive then who has any descendants today is an ancestor of every human on Earth right now.
facts.angle: a family tree that collapses into everyone
facts.whatif: How far back do you and a total stranger share a common ancestor? Astonishingly little. The math of doubling ancestors means that just a few thousand years ago, the same people were forefathers of the entire modern human race.
facts.wow: It means everyone alive, of every background, is at least a distant cousin, all branches of one recent tree.

facts.fact: The Sahara, the largest hot desert on Earth, was a green land of lakes, rivers, and hippos just a few thousand years ago. Ancient rock art there even shows people swimming.
facts.angle: the world's emptiest place was once its lushest
facts.whatif: What did the Sahara look like when the first pyramids were being planned? Not endless sand, but a wet savanna full of grazing animals and human settlements. A slow wobble in Earth's orbit dried it out into the desert we know.
facts.wow: Cave paintings deep in the Sahara still show people swimming, in a place where it now almost never rains.

facts.fact: The wood frog survives winter by freezing almost solid — its heart stops, it stops breathing, and up to two-thirds of the water in its body turns to ice. In spring it thaws and hops away, alive.
facts.angle: an animal that comes back from the dead
facts.whatif: What if you froze solid — no heartbeat, no breath — for weeks, then simply came back to life? The wood frog does exactly that every winter, flooding its cells with glucose so the ice can't destroy them.
facts.wow: By any normal definition it is dead for weeks, yet when the ice melts its heart restarts on its own and it hops away.

facts.fact: Your stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve metal, so to avoid digesting itself your stomach grows a brand-new lining every few days.
facts.whatif: What if the acid in your stomach ever touched the stomach wall directly? It would start dissolving you — so your body rebuilds the entire protective lining every three to four days.
facts.wow: The same acid that breaks down dinner would happily break down your stomach; the only thing saving you is a layer of mucus and cells you replace constantly.

facts.fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the first Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
facts.angle: history is far older than it feels
facts.whatif: What if the pyramids were already ancient ruins when Cleopatra was alive? They were — the Great Pyramid was finished around 2,500 years before her, while the Moon landing was only about 2,000 years after.
facts.wow: We picture Cleopatra and the pyramid-builders together, but she lived closer to the age of spaceflight than to the workers who stacked those stones.

facts.fact: Wombats are the only animals on Earth that produce cube-shaped poop — up to a hundred little cubes a night.
facts.whatif: What if your poop came out as neat little cubes? A wombat's does, because the last stretch of its intestine has stiff and stretchy patches that mould the waste into six-sided blocks.
facts.wow: They stack the cubes on rocks and logs to mark territory, and the cubes don't roll away — which is likely the whole point.

facts.fact: A cockroach can live for weeks without its head. It doesn't die from losing it — it dies of thirst.
facts.whatif: What if losing your head barely slowed you down? A cockroach breathes through holes in its body, not its mouth, and its simple nervous system keeps working — so a headless one can still stand and react for weeks.
facts.wow: It only dies because, without a mouth, it can't drink — so it slowly dehydrates.

facts.angle: time is bigger than you think
facts.fact: Pluto has not completed a single orbit of the Sun since humans discovered it in 1930 — and it won't until 2178.
facts.whatif: What if a whole planet hadn't finished one 'year' since your great-grandparents were young? Pluto takes 248 Earth years to circle the Sun, so its year that began at discovery is barely half over.
facts.wow: Everyone who was alive when Pluto was found will be long gone before it returns to the same spot in its orbit.

facts.fact: Your left lung is smaller than your right — it has a permanent dent carved out to make room for your heart.
facts.whatif: What if your two lungs were never meant to match? The left one has two lobes instead of three and a scooped-out notch, because your heart sits slightly to the left and needs the space.
facts.wow: You've been breathing with two mismatched lungs your entire life and never noticed.

facts.fact: Your gut has its own brain — a network of about 500 million neurons that keeps working even if it's cut off from your head.
facts.whatif: What if your stomach could think for itself? The gut's own nervous system, the size of a cat's brain, runs digestion on its own and talks to your head constantly — which is why fear gives you 'butterflies'.
facts.wow: Most of your body's serotonin, the 'feel-good' chemical, is made in your gut, not your brain.

facts.fact: Some bamboo plants flower only once every hundred-plus years — and then every plant of that species, all over the world, flowers and dies at the same time.
facts.whatif: What if plants split across different continents somehow knew to bloom on the exact same year? Bamboo of the same species does, following an internal clock set a century ago from a single parent.
facts.wow: They're genetic clones running the same countdown, so they flower together, drop their seeds, and die together — an event people wait lifetimes to see.

facts.fact: Deep in the Amazon there is a river so hot it boils — hot enough to cook animals that fall in.
facts.whatif: What if a river in the middle of a rainforest, nowhere near a volcano, ran near boiling? The Shanay-timpishka does, heated by water forced up from deep underground.
facts.wow: Locals considered it sacred long before scientists confirmed a nearly four-kilometre stretch that steams and scalds.

facts.angle: time is bigger than you think
facts.fact: Oxford University was already teaching students before the Aztec Empire even existed.
facts.whatif: What if one of the world's famous 'ancient' civilizations was younger than a university still running today? Oxford had classes by 1096, while the Aztec capital wasn't founded until the 1300s.
facts.wow: Students were sitting exams at Oxford centuries before the first stone of the Aztec capital was laid.

facts.fact: You can't tickle yourself — and the reason reveals something strange about how your brain works.
facts.whatif: What if your brain quietly erased sensations it caused itself? When you move your own hand, your cerebellum predicts the touch and cancels it out, so the surprise that makes tickling work never happens.
facts.wow: It's the same prediction system that lets you tell the difference between the world shaking and you shaking your own head.

facts.fact: A fungus can hijack an ant's body, march it to the perfect spot, and force it to bite down before killing it and sprouting from its head.
facts.whatif: What if a fungus could drive a living body like a puppet? Ophiocordyceps infects an ant, steers it to a leaf at just the right height and humidity, and makes it clamp on in a 'death grip'.
facts.wow: Then it kills the ant and grows a stalk out of its head to rain spores on the colony below — the real inspiration for zombie fiction.

facts.fact: There's a place where lightning strikes almost every night of the year, for hours at a time — up to 260 nights a year.
facts.whatif: What if there were a spot on Earth that was basically a permanent lightning storm? Over Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, warm air and mountain winds collide to fire near-endless lightning after dark.
facts.wow: It flashes so reliably that sailors once used it as a natural lighthouse to navigate.

facts.fact: A diamond and the 'lead' in your pencil are made of the exact same thing — pure carbon. The only difference is how the atoms are stacked.
facts.whatif: What if the hardest natural material and one of the softest were secretly identical? Diamond and pencil graphite are both nothing but carbon; rearrange the bonds and one becomes the other.
facts.wow: With enough heat and pressure, that pencil mark could, in principle, become a diamond.

facts.fact: Light normally races at 300 million metres a second — but scientists have slowed it to the speed of a bicycle, and even brought it to a complete stop.
facts.whatif: What if the fastest thing in the universe could be made to crawl? By chilling atoms to near absolute zero, physicists slowed a light beam to about the pace of a rush-hour cyclist.
facts.wow: They've even frozen a pulse of light in place, stored it, and released it again moments later — like catching a sunbeam in a jar.

facts.fact: When lightning hits sand, it can instantly melt it into a jagged tube of glass — a frozen scar shaped like the bolt itself.
facts.whatif: What if you could hold the shape of a lightning strike in your hand? Where a bolt slams into sand, the heat fuses grains into a hollow glass tube called a fulgurite, tracing the path the electricity took underground.
facts.wow: Some of these lightning-glass tubes branch metres down into the earth, a permanent cast of a single instant.

facts.fact: Mushrooms can connect trees and plants through underground networks, allowing them to share nutrients and information. This network can even help plants warn each other of potential threats.
facts.whatif: What if these networks could be used to create more resilient ecosystems? Could we use them to help plants adapt to changing environments?
facts.wow: Some of these networks can cover hundreds of acres, making them some of the largest living organisms on the planet.

facts.fact: Humans have a forgotten sense that allows us to detect the Earth's magnetic field. This sense is thought to be linked to the way some animals migrate.
facts.whatif: What if we could harness this sense to improve our navigation abilities? Could it help us develop new technologies for navigation?
facts.wow: Some researchers believe that this sense may be linked to the way some people can detect changes in the weather.

facts.fact: Deep sea vents can create entire ecosystems that thrive in the harsh conditions surrounding them. These ecosystems can support unique and diverse life forms.
facts.whatif: What if these ecosystems could provide clues to the origins of life on Earth? Could they help us understand how life can thrive in extreme environments?
facts.wow: Some of these vents can support giant tube worms that can grow up to 8 feet long, making them one of the most extreme examples of life on the planet.

facts.fact: The branching patterns of trees can be described using mathematical equations. These equations can help us understand how trees grow and adapt to their environments.
facts.whatif: What if these mathematical patterns could be used to improve our understanding of other natural systems? Could they help us develop new technologies for sustainable growth?
facts.wow: Some researchers have used these equations to create computer simulations of tree growth, allowing us to study and predict the behavior of entire forests.

facts.fact: Fungi can solve mazes and make decisions based on their environment. This intelligence is thought to be linked to the way they grow and adapt to their surroundings.
facts.whatif: What if this intelligence could be harnessed to develop new technologies for problem-solving? Could it help us create more efficient and adaptive systems?
facts.wow: Some fungi can even infect and control the behavior of insects, using them to help spread their own spores.

facts.fact: The speed of light is the universal speed limit, and nothing can reach or exceed it. This limit has been consistently observed and confirmed through experiments.
facts.whatif: What if this limit could be used to develop new technologies for space travel? Could it help us create faster and more efficient propulsion systems?
facts.wow: The speed of light is so fast that it can circle the Earth over 7 times in just one second.

facts.fact: The Earth's magnetic field is thought to be generated by the movement of molten iron in the Earth's core. This field plays a crucial role in protecting the planet from harmful solar and cosmic radiation.
facts.whatif: What if this field could be used to develop new technologies for shielding and protection? Could it help us create more secure and resilient systems?
facts.wow: The Earth's magnetic field is so strong that it can trap and hold charged particles from the solar wind, creating spectacular displays of the aurora borealis.

facts.fact: Some materials can exhibit unique properties, such as superconductivity or superfluidity, under certain conditions. These properties can be harnessed to develop new technologies and applications.
facts.whatif: What if these materials could be used to develop new technologies for energy transmission and storage? Could they help us create more efficient and sustainable systems?
facts.wow: Some materials can even exhibit negative mass, where they respond to forces in the opposite way of regular matter.

facts.fact: Weather patterns can be influenced by the movement of the Earth's oceans and the atmosphere. These patterns can have a significant impact on the climate and ecosystems of our planet.
facts.whatif: What if these patterns could be used to develop new technologies for weather forecasting and prediction? Could they help us create more accurate and reliable models?
facts.wow: Some weather patterns, such as El Niño and La Niña, can have a significant impact on global climate and food production.

facts.fact: Our senses can be deceived by our brains, which can create illusions and misperceptions of reality. This deception can be influenced by our expectations, emotions, and past experiences.
facts.whatif: What if this deception could be used to develop new technologies for sensory enhancement and manipulation? Could it help us create more realistic and immersive experiences?
facts.wow: Some illusions can be so powerful that they can create entirely new sensations, such as the feeling of touch or movement.

facts.fact: Chemical reactions can be influenced by the presence of catalysts, which can speed up or slow down the reaction. These catalysts can be used to develop new technologies and applications.
facts.whatif: What if these catalysts could be used to develop new technologies for energy production and storage? Could they help us create more efficient and sustainable systems?
facts.wow: Some catalysts can even be used to create entirely new materials, such as nanomaterials and metamaterials.

facts.whatif: What if humans could also transform their bodies to bypass aging and death? Would we still experience the same emotions and connections with others?
